eras.title: British Invasion, Motown, and soul
eras.basis: Anchored to the Billboard Hot 100 archive — every chart week since 1958 is browsable, and each pick here held the #1 spot.
eras.summary: When The Beatles hit America in early 1964 they opened the door for a British Invasion, but the charts they stormed were shared ground: The Supremes and the Motown hit machine answered from Detroit, and by decade's end Aretha Franklin, Marvin Gaye, and Sly and the Family Stone had made soul the sound of American radio.

eras.title: Punk vs. the pop charts
eras.basis: Anchored to the Official Charts Company archive — every UK chart week since 1952 is browsable.
eras.summary: Punk detonated in Britain while the singles chart stayed stubbornly mainstream: Sex Pistols' God Save the Queen was famously held at #2 in Jubilee week 1977 while Wings' Mull of Kintyre became the first UK single to sell two million. Donna Summer's I Feel Love pointed at the dance future, and by 1979 punk's new-wave children — Ian Dury and the Blockheads, Blondie — were topping the chart itself.

eras.title: Ska, rocksteady, and the birth of reggae
eras.basis: Jamaica's radio charts from this era barely survive — this snapshot draws on documented sound-system and studio history.
eras.summary: Jamaica's hits were made in the dance, not on a sales chart: Kingston sound systems run by producers like Coxsone Dodd and Duke Reid decided what the island moved to. Derrick Morgan and Prince Buster ruled the ska years, The Wailers' Simmer Down announced a new generation, and when the beat slowed in 1966, Alton Ellis and Hopeton Lewis made rocksteady the sound of Kingston. By 1968 Toots and the Maytals had given the next thing its name — reggae — and deejays like U-Roy turned the sound system itself into an instrument.

eras.title: The yé-yé years
eras.basis: France had no official chart before November 1984 — this snapshot follows Salut les copains-era documentation; pre-1984 chart positions are later reconstructions.
eras.summary: France's arbiter wasn't a chart — official charts only began in 1984 — it was Salut les copains, the radio show and million-selling magazine that crowned the yé-yé generation. Johnny Hallyday and Sylvie Vartan were its royal couple, Françoise Hardy turned Tous les garçons et les filles into the bedroom anthem of a generation, and France Gall took yé-yé to Eurovision victory in 1965. When Salut les copains threw a free concert at Place de la Nation in 1963, some 150,000 kids showed up.

eras.title: Schlager, Anglo pop — and a krautrock underground
eras.basis: Anchored to the German number-one archives; the split between what charted and what was later canonized is documented music history.
eras.summary: West Germany's charts told an honest, unglamorous truth: the country bought schlager and international pop. Vicky Leandros and Heino ruled the German-language side while George Harrison and ABBA took the #1 spots from abroad. The krautrock now canonized worldwide — Can, Neu!, Faust — barely touched the domestic charts at the time; the great exception was Kraftwerk, whose Autobahn drove into the German top ten and changed pop's future.

eras.title: La Movida and the pop boom
eras.basis: Spain's official sales chart only starts in 1986 — this snapshot draws on documented Movida history and the Los 40 Principales airplay era.
eras.summary: After Franco, Madrid exploded. La Movida Madrileña turned the city into an all-night laboratory: Alaska fronting Pegamoides and then Dinarama, Radio Futura, and Nacha Pop — whose Chica de ayer became the movement's signature song. The honest footnote: Spain's best-selling pop of the decade belonged to Mecano and Hombres G, the chart-friendly edge of the same generation.

eras.title: Streaming takes the chart
eras.basis: Anchored to the Billboard Hot 100 archive — the streaming-era chart, browsable week by week.
eras.summary: By the mid-2010s the Hot 100 counted streams, and America's chart moved at internet speed. Mark Ronson and Bruno Mars opened the era with retro-funk, Adele's Hello proved the event single still worked, Drake made streaming dominance routine, Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee's Despacito held #1 for sixteen weeks — and Lil Nas X's Old Town Road, a country-rap single born as a meme, outlasted them all with the longest #1 run in the chart's history.

eras.title: Streaming Britain
eras.basis: Anchored to the Official Charts Company archive; the UK chart has counted streams alongside sales since 2014.
eras.summary: Britain's chart started counting streams in 2014, and the late 2010s belonged to the artists who mastered the new mathematics: Ed Sheeran's Shape of You logged fourteen weeks at #1 in 2017, Drake's One Dance managed fifteen the year before, and Adele's Hello proved the old-fashioned event single still worked. By decade's end, homegrown voices closed the era — Stormzy took UK rap to #1 with Vossi Bop, and Lewis Capaldi's Someone You Loved held on for seven weeks.

eras.title: The chart at feed speed
eras.basis: Anchored to the Billboard Hot 100 archive, documented week by week through the present.
eras.summary: The 2020s Hot 100 moves at the speed of the feed. The Weeknd's Blinding Lights opened the decade and never seemed to leave the chart, Olivia Rodrigo's Drivers License made her a star overnight, and K-pop planted its flag — BTS's Butter held ten weeks in 2021, and in 2025 Golden, sung by HUNTR/X, the fictional trio from KPop Demon Hunters, topped the real chart for eight. Shaboozey's A Bar Song (Tipsy) tied the all-time nineteen-week record, and Kendrick Lamar and SZA's Luther held on for thirteen. In 2026 the long run came from Nashville again: Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas kept returning to the Hot 100 summit — breaking the all-time record with its twenty-third week in September and reaching twenty-four by October — while Taylor Swift's I Knew It, I Knew You, from Toy Story 5, became her fifteenth #1, more than any artist this century.

eras.title: Streaming Britain, homegrown edition
eras.basis: Anchored to the Official Charts Company archive, documented week by week through the present.
eras.summary: Britain's 2020s chart is a streaming ledger with a local accent. Dave and Central Cee's Sprinter gave UK rap a ten-week #1 in 2023, Ed Sheeran kept his grip with Bad Habits, and Miley Cyrus's Flowers matched Sprinter's ten weeks the same year. Sabrina Carpenter stacked twenty-one #1 weeks in a single calendar year — a record for a female artist — and in 2025 Alex Warren's Ordinary ran twelve straight weeks, the longest uninterrupted UK #1 ever by a US male solo artist. Then 2026 broke the oldest record on the board: Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's Rein Me In kept returning to #1 from February into September — twenty-three non-consecutive weeks in all, longer than any single in the chart's history — before Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas took a single week at the top in September and Taylor Swift's Patient Zero arrived in October.

eras.title: Shanties, party schlager, and rap royalty
eras.basis: Anchored to Germany's official chart archives (GfK Entertainment), via the year-by-year number-one lists.
eras.summary: Germany's 2020s chart swung between internet moments and homegrown giants. Nathan Evans' sea shanty Wellerman sailed off TikTok to #1 in 2021; the party-schlager Layla by DJ Robin and Schürze topped the chart in 2022 even as cities like Würzburg kept it off their volksfest stages; and in 2023 Udo Lindenberg, German rock's elder statesman, joined rapper Apache 207 on Komet — #1 for 21 non-consecutive weeks, the longest-running German chart-topper of all time. In summer 2026 the chart stood still: Shakira and Burna Boy's Dai Dai held #1 for thirteen straight weeks from July through September, until Taylor Swift's Patient Zero ended the run in October.

eras.title: The Oricon years — enka, novelty, and the folk turn
eras.basis: Japan had no national pop chart until Oricon's began on 4 January 1968; every ranking here is counted week by week from Oricon's weekly number-one tables (reproduced from Oricon No.1 Hits 500, Clubhouse 1998), cross-checked against per-song sources.
eras.summary: Japan's first real pop chart opened on 4 January 1968, and its very first number one was Los Primos' "Love You Tokyo" — a nightclub ballad, not the guitar bands then filling the Budokan. That gap is the era's whole story: Group Sounds had the youth and the headlines, but the chart belonged to kayōkyoku and enka. The Folk Crusaders took five weeks with a novelty about a drunk in heaven; Ayumi Ishida held nine with "Blue Light Yokohama"; and the country's biggest record of 1970 was a schoolboy, Osamu Minagawa, singing a translated Italian children's song about a black cat for fourteen straight weeks. Then Keiko Fuji did something the chart has rarely seen since — eighteen consecutive weeks at number one across two different singles, one handing straight off to the next. The outright record went to Shiro Miya to Pinkara Trio: sixteen unbroken weeks with "Onna no Michi", and the annual number one two years running. Underneath, a quieter argument was reshaping everything. The folk boom put Takuro Yoshida and Kaguyahime on the chart singing plainly about cheap inns and small rooms by the Kanda river, while Nobuyasu Okabayashi — whose protest songs were widely banned from broadcast — was being called the Japanese Dylan. Happy End never charted at all, and still changed the most: their 1970–71 albums set off the nihongo rock ronsō, the public argument over whether rock could be sung in Japanese, and settled it by example.

eras.title: From the Hep Stars to ABBA — the Kvällstoppen years
eras.basis: Kvällstoppen was Sveriges Radio's weekly sales list from 10 July 1962 to 19 August 1975, ranking the twenty best-selling records from selected shops with singles and albums in one chart; every week count here is read from the Swedish Wikipedia list of its number ones, cross-checked against per-song pages.
eras.summary: Sweden's sales chart was a year old when The Beatles played their first shows outside Britain — a school hall in Karlstad on 25 October 1963, then Stockholm and Gothenburg — and a month later She Loves You gave the list its first Beatles number one. Every chart-topper had been in English until December 1964, when Sven-Ingvars took Fröken Fräken to the top. The homegrown beat boom came next: The Hep Stars, with a young Benny Andersson on organ, put three of his own songs at number one in 1966 and held it nine straight weeks with Consolation, while Gothenburg's Tages, often rated the best Swedish band of the era, were the rivals. Swedish-language pop kept its foothold — Anna-Lena Löfgren's Lyckliga gatan, a translation of Adriano Celentano's Il ragazzo della via Gluck, ran six weeks in early 1968, and the week it ended Agnetha Fältskog had her first number one. Because singles and albums shared one chart, the early 1970s belong to LPs: Ted Gärdestad's debut Undringar, with the four future members of ABBA playing and singing behind him, held ten weeks in 1972, and Hoola Bandoola Band, a progg group on the MNW label, sat at number one for a month in 1973 — on the very sales chart that the progg movement, with its open contempt for the pop of Stikkan Anderson and ABBA, defined itself against. Then came the pivot. ABBA, still billed as Björn, Benny, Agnetha & Frida, had six weeks with Ring Ring in 1973 after finishing third in the Eurovision selection; in 1974 Waterloo won Melodifestivalen on 9 February, won Eurovision in Brighton on 6 April, and the album held number one for twelve weeks while the single sat behind it at two and three. The chart's last spring belonged to Björn Skifs' Michelangelo and to ABBA's self-titled album, sixteen weeks at the top, even as the progg scene staged its Alternativfestivalen in a Stockholm tent in March 1975 as a protest against Melodifestivalen and everything it stood for.

eras.title: The Go-Set years — from Friday on My Mind to Eagle Rock
eras.basis: Australia's first national pop chart ran in the Melbourne weekly Go-Set from 5 October 1966 until the paper closed on 24 August 1974; week counts here come from Go-Set's own number-one table as republished online with its chart compiler's permission, and differ in places from David Kent's later retro-calculated charts.
eras.summary: Australia had no national chart until Go-Set, a Melbourne teen weekly, printed one on 5 October 1966 with Yellow Submarine at number one. Three months later The Easybeats took Friday on My Mind to the top for a single week — the song an industry panel would name the best Australian song ever written, in 2001. The Seekers came home in March 1967 to an estimated 200,000 people at Melbourne's Myer Music Bowl and had the year's biggest single with Georgy Girl; Johnny Farnham followed with a novelty about a cleaning lady, his first solo single, five weeks at number one and the top record of 1968. Russell Morris' The Real Thing — Johnny Young's song stretched to six minutes by producer Ian "Molly" Meldrum — was 1969's. Then the industry went to war with itself: from May to October 1970 commercial radio refused to play major-label British and Australian records in a pay-for-play dispute, Go-Set switched to surveying record shops directly, and The Mixtures' cover of In the Summertime on the minor Fable label held number one for nine weeks. Daddy Cool's Eagle Rock, a debut single, ran ten weeks in 1971 and their album became the first Australian LP to sell 100,000 copies. Local acts thinned out at the top after the ban — Blackfeather was one of only two Australian number ones in 1972 — and Go-Set's final chart, in August 1974, belonged to Paper Lace. David Kent's Kent Music Report, launched that May, became the official chart; Countdown went to air on the ABC on 8 November 1974; and Skyhooks had just released Living in the 70's with six of its ten tracks banned from commercial radio.

eras.title: From Sanremo to the cantautori — the Musica e dischi years
eras.basis: Weeks at #1 are read from Musica e dischi's own archive of its weekly best-selling-singles chart, compiled from 1959/60, and cross-read against the Hit Parade Italia-based year lists on Wikipedia; where the two disagree, the Musica e dischi figure is used and said so.
eras.summary: In 1964 the Sanremo festival still made each song be sung twice, by an Italian and a foreign guest, and Bobby Solo was thrown out of it for singing to a backing track — then held #1 for nine weeks anyway, while sixteen-year-old Gigliola Cinquetti won Sanremo and Eurovision in the same spring. The beat boom followed: Little Tony's Elvis act, Caterina Caselli out-selling the festival winner, and the Italian-language covers of foreign hits that filled the chart (Mina's biggest record of the span was a Nino Ferrer song). By 1968 Patty Pravo had nine weeks on top with La bambola, and Paolo Conte had written Azzurro for Adriano Celentano. Then the songwriters took the chart: Lucio Dalla's 4/3/1943 out-sold the 1971 Sanremo winner by the compiler's count, and Lucio Battisti's Pensieri e parole sat at #1 for fourteen summer weeks. Fabrizio De André never appears in these #1 tables; the cantautori who did were Battisti and Dalla. Two archives cover these years and often disagree on week counts — the numbers here follow the compiler's own.

eras.title: Veronica’s Top 40 — from the pirate ship to Hilversum
eras.basis: Every peak, week count and date is read from the Dutch Top 40’s own archive (Stichting Nederlandse Top 40, top40.nl): the weekly lists for each week at #1, the song pages and the compiler’s chart-position data; Wikipedia’s per-year number-one lists cross-read, with the one disagreement said so on the item.
eras.summary: The Dutch Top 40 went on air on 2 January 1965 from the offshore pirate Radio Veronica, the idea of its DJ Joost den Draaijer after the American radio charts, with the Beatles’ I Feel Fine at number one. The Hague was the country’s beat capital — the Golden Earrings, Q65 and the Motions formed there, and Shocking Blue in 1967 — and the chart of these years is theirs as much as anyone’s: Golden Earring on top with Back Home in 1970 and Radar Love in 1973, Boudewijn de Groot singing Dutch, The Cats from Volendam, Tee-Set and Mouth & MacNeal. Shocking Blue’s Venus never passed #3 at home, then became the first US number one by a Dutch band in February 1970. On Saturday 31 August 1974 at six in the evening Veronica switched off, the day before the anti-pirate law took effect; former Veronica staff had already set up the Stichting Nederlandse Top 40, and from October the TROS carried the list on Hilversum 3 as the Nederlandse Top 40 — the chart outlived the ship.

eras.title: RPM and the CanCon years
eras.basis: Every week count and date is read from the table rows of Wikipedia's per-year lists of RPM number ones and checked against scans of the RPM issues themselves (RPM, the Toronto trade weekly Walt Grealis founded in February 1964); Library and Archives Canada's RPM database refused automated reads, so the scans stand in for it.
eras.summary: RPM, the Toronto trade weekly that Walt Grealis started in February 1964, began printing its Top Forty-5s chart in its 22 June 1964 issue, with the Dixie Cups' Chapel of Love at number one. In March 1965 the Winnipeg band Chad Allan and the Expressions took Shakin' All Over to #1 after their label credited the single to "Guess Who?" — disc jockeys kept using the name, and the group became The Guess Who. Five years later their American Woman topped RPM's chart and the Billboard Hot 100 in the same three weeks from 9 May 1970, the first Hot 100 number one by a Canadian band. On 18 January 1971 rules came into force requiring AM radio stations to devote 30 percent of their music to Canadian content, a cause RPM had led, and from that year Canadian titles on its chart carried the MAPL logo Stan Klees designed. In 1974 alone six Canadian acts — Terry Jacks, Gordon Lightfoot, Anne Murray, Andy Kim, Paul Anka and Bachman–Turner Overdrive — each had an RPM number one.
